title: ArrayDeque replaces Stack: push/pop/peek LIFO behavior
keyPoints: ArrayDeque provides push(), pop(), and peek() for proper LIFO stack behavior without synchronization overhead
Stack extends Vector, making every method synchronized even in single-threaded code, adding 15-30% overhead
Stack exposes get(index) and other Vector methods that violate the LIFO abstraction of a stack
ArrayDeque's push adds to the head, pop removes from the head, and peek reads the head without removing
Always declare as Deque<T> interface, not the ArrayDeque class, for loose coupling
ArrayDeque does not allow null elements; Stack (via Vector) does

s1_definition.oneliner: ArrayDeque provides push/pop/peek for LIFO stack behavior backed by a circular array, replacing the legacy Stack class which extends synchronized Vector and exposes non-stack methods.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **push(e)** adds to the head of the deque (top of the stack) in O(1) amortized
- **pop()** removes from the head in O(1); throws `NoSuchElementException` if empty
- **peek()** reads the head without removing in O(1); returns null if empty
- Stack's problems: synchronized every method (slow), extends Vector (exposes get/set/add by index), legacy API (search returns 1-based position)
- The Java Javadoc explicitly states: "This class is likely to be faster than Stack when used as a stack"
s1_definition.analogy: Stack (legacy) is like an old safe with a heavy lock that opens and closes for every single operation – even when only one person uses it. Worse, the safe has a side window that lets you grab items from any position, which is not how a stack should work. ArrayDeque is a modern spring-loaded tray: put on top (push), take from top (pop), look at the top (peek). No lock, no side access, proper LIFO behavior.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Stack vs ArrayDeque

  Stack (legacy):
  ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
  │ push(e) → synchronized add     │
  │ pop()   → synchronized remove  │
  │ peek()  → synchronized read    │
  │ get(i)  → random access!       │ ← violates LIFO
  │ search()→ 1-based position     │ ← non-standard
  └─────────────────────────────────┘

  ArrayDeque (modern):
  ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
  │ push(e) → addFirst (no lock)   │
  │ pop()   → removeFirst (no lock)│
  │ peek()  → peekFirst (no lock)  │
  │ No get(i), no random access    │ ← proper LIFO
  └─────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
ArrayDeque is the modern replacement for the legacy Stack class. It provides the same push, pop, and peek operations for LIFO behavior, but without the synchronization overhead and without the leaky abstraction of random access.

Stack extends Vector, which means every operation acquires a monitor lock even when only one thread uses the stack. Worse, Stack inherits Vector's get, set, and add-by-index methods, which break the fundamental contract of a stack: only the top element should be accessible.

In the National Bank of India's account management system, Rajesh uses `Deque<String> undoStack = new ArrayDeque<>()` for the undo feature. When Rajesh changes an account's address, the old address is pushed onto the stack. Undoing the change pops the stack and restores the previous value. ArrayDeque handles this 2-3x faster than Stack with half the memory.

Remember one sentence: always use `Deque<T> stack = new ArrayDeque<>()` for stack behavior – never the Stack class.
